q: Under ASC 958 as amended by ASU 2016-14, how must a not-for-profit organization classify its net assets on the statement of financial position?
choices: Net assets with donor restrictions and net assets without donor restrictions
Unrestricted, temporarily restricted, and permanently restricted
Operating and nonoperating net assets
Board-designated and undesignated net assets
exp: ASU 2016-14 replaced the three classes with two: with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions. Board designations are disclosed within net assets without donor restrictions, since boards cannot impose donor restrictions.

q: In December, Year 1, a donor made an unconditional written pledge of $50,000 to Hope Shelter, payable in March, Year 2, with no stated purpose restriction. How should Hope report the pledge in Year 1?
choices: No revenue until the cash is received
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions
Deferred revenue (a liability)
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions
exp: An unconditional promise to give is recognized as revenue when received. A pledge payable in a future period carries an implied time restriction, so it is reported as with donor restrictions until received (ASC 958-605-45-5). Waiting for the cash applies the rule for conditional promises.

q: A foundation promised River Museum $200,000, but only if the museum raises $200,000 from other donors by December 31; if the museum fails, the foundation will give nothing. By December 31, the museum had raised $120,000 from others. How much of the foundation's promise should the museum recognize as revenue for the year?
exp: The promise contains a barrier (the matching requirement) and a release from obligation, so it is conditional and recognized only when the barrier is overcome (ASU 2018-08). Because the match is all-or-nothing and was not met, no revenue is recognized; $120,000 would apply only if the match were dollar-for-dollar.

q: During the year, a CPA volunteered tax services to Bright Futures, an NFP, that it would otherwise have purchased for $10,000. Volunteers also staffed a fundraising phone bank; their services were worth $15,000 at minimum wage. What amount of contributed services should Bright Futures recognize?
exp: Contributed services are recognized only if they create or enhance nonfinancial assets, or require specialized skills, are provided by people with those skills, and would typically be purchased if not donated (ASC 958-605-25-16). The CPA's services qualify; the phone bank volunteers' do not.

q: In Year 1, Care Clinic received a $50,000 cash gift restricted by the donor to its immunization program. During Year 1, the clinic spent $30,000 on immunizations. How should the expense and restriction be reported?
choices: Expense of $30,000 in net assets without donor restrictions, and $30,000 of net assets released from restrictions
Expense of $30,000 in net assets with donor restrictions
Expense of $50,000 in net assets without donor restrictions
No expense until the full $50,000 is spent
exp: All expenses are reported in net assets without donor restrictions. Fulfilling the purpose restriction releases $30,000, reported as a reclassification from with to without donor restrictions (ASC 958-205-45). Expenses are never reported in the with-donor-restrictions class.

q: Under ASU 2016-14, which not-for-profit organizations must present an analysis of expenses by both function and nature?
choices: Only voluntary health and welfare organizations
Only NFPs with revenue above $1 million
Only NFPs that receive federal grants
All not-for-profit organizations
exp: ASU 2016-14 extended the requirement to all NFPs; the analysis may be presented on the face of the statement of activities, as a separate statement, or in the notes. Before the amendment only voluntary health and welfare organizations had to present a statement of functional expenses.

q: How should a not-for-profit organization report its investment return on the statement of activities?
choices: Gross investment income, with all investment expenses reported as management and general expense
Net of external and direct internal investment expenses
Only realized gains, with unrealized gains in a separate statement
Net of all expenses, including fundraising costs
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires investment return to be presented net of external and direct internal investment expenses, and no longer requires disclosure of the netted expenses. Fundraising costs are never netted against investment return.

q: A university's donor-restricted endowment fund has a fair value below the original gift amount (it is underwater). Where should the deficiency be reported under ASU 2016-14?
choices: In net assets without donor restrictions
As a liability to the donor
In net assets with donor restrictions
As a reduction of board-designated endowment
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires underwater amounts of donor-restricted endowments to be reported within net assets with donor restrictions, with expanded disclosures. Before the amendment, deficiencies were charged to unrestricted net assets.

q: Art League, an NFP, charges members $100 per year in dues. Members receive benefits (magazine, admission, discounts) with a fair value of about $100. How should Art League account for the dues under ASU 2018-08?
choices: As contribution revenue when received
As contribution revenue with donor restrictions
As a liability until the member terminates membership
As exchange revenue recognized over the membership period
exp: When the resource provider receives commensurate value in return, the transaction is an exchange, not a contribution, and revenue is recognized under ASC 606 as the benefits are provided. Dues are a contribution only to the extent they exceed the value of benefits received.

q: Hope Hospital Foundation held a gala, selling 400 tickets at $250 each. The fair value of the dinner and entertainment provided to each attendee was $100. How should the foundation report the ticket revenue?
choices: Contribution revenue of $60,000 and special event (exchange) revenue of $40,000
Contribution revenue of $100,000
Special event revenue of $100,000
Contribution revenue of $40,000 and exchange revenue of $60,000
exp: Each $250 ticket includes a $100 exchange (the dinner) and a $150 contribution: 400 x $150 = $60,000 contribution and 400 x $100 = $40,000 exchange revenue. Reversing the amounts allocates the contribution to the value of benefits received.

q: City Charity received $100,000 from a donor with instructions to transfer it to a specified food bank. City Charity has no variance power and cannot redirect the funds. How should City Charity account for the receipt?
choices: Contribution revenue with donor restrictions
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions
An asset and a liability to the food bank
Disclosure only
exp: A recipient acting as an agent or intermediary without variance power reports the assets and a liability to the specified beneficiary, not contribution revenue (ASC 958-605-25-24). Revenue would be recognized only if City Charity had variance power.

q: United Fund received $500,000 from a donor who designated a specific agency as the beneficiary but explicitly granted United Fund unilateral power to redirect the gift to another beneficiary. How should United Fund account for the receipt?
choices: As a liability to the designated agency
As contribution revenue
As an agency transaction with no effect on the statement of activities
As deferred revenue until the funds are distributed
exp: When the donor explicitly grants variance power, the recipient organization recognizes the asset and contribution revenue (ASC 958-605-25-25). Liability treatment applies when the recipient lacks variance power.

q: Under ASC 958-360 as amended by ASU 2019-03, a museum need not capitalize contributed works of art in its collection if certain conditions are met. Which of the following is one of those conditions?
choices: The items have a fair value below $5,000
The items were acquired by purchase rather than donation
The museum discloses the items' fair value in the notes
Proceeds from sales of collection items are used to acquire other collection items or for direct care of existing collections, per organizational policy
exp: Collection items need not be capitalized if they are held for public exhibition, education, or research for public service, are protected and preserved, and are subject to a policy requiring sale proceeds to be used for acquisitions or direct care (ASU 2019-03 added direct care). There is no dollar threshold.

q: Which of the following is true regarding depreciation of long-lived assets by not-for-profit organizations?
choices: NFPs must recognize depreciation on long-lived tangible assets, but not on individual works of art or historical treasures with extraordinarily long lives
NFPs may elect not to record depreciation
Only NFPs that charge fees for services must record depreciation
Depreciation is recognized only for donated assets
exp: ASC 958-360-35 requires NFPs to depreciate long-lived assets, with an exception for individual works of art or historical treasures whose economic benefit is used up slowly. There is no general option to omit depreciation.

q: Green Trust, an NFP, received a $2,000,000 cash contribution restricted by the donor to constructing a new building. How should the receipt be classified in the statement of cash flows?
choices: Operating activities
Investing activities
Financing activities
Noncash investing and financing activities
exp: Cash contributions restricted by donors for long-term purposes, such as acquiring buildings or establishing endowments, are financing inflows (ASC 230-10-45-14). Unrestricted contributions are operating, and the later construction payments are investing.

q: Hope Shelter paid $40,000 for a direct-mail fundraising campaign in December. The campaign is expected to generate contributions throughout the following year. How should the cost be reported?
choices: As a prepaid asset amortized as contributions are received
As fundraising expense when incurred
As a reduction of contribution revenue
As a program service expense
exp: Fundraising costs are expensed as incurred, even if they are expected to produce contributions in future periods (ASC 958-720-25-4). Netting them against contribution revenue is not permitted.

q: A not-for-profit mails a brochure that includes both an educational message and a request for donations. Which criteria must all be met for part of the joint costs to be allocated to program activities rather than fundraising?
choices: Purpose, audience, and content
Cost, benefit, and materiality
Timing, frequency, and audience
Donor intent, board approval, and content
exp: Under ASC 958-720-45, joint costs may be allocated to program or management functions only if the purpose, audience, and content criteria are all met; otherwise all joint costs are fundraising. Board approval is not a criterion.

q: A donor contributed a building with a fair value of $1,500,000 to Youth Center, an NFP, with no stipulations about its use or how long it must be used. Youth Center has no policy implying time restrictions. How should the contribution be reported?
choices: Contribution revenue with donor restrictions, released over the building's useful life
No revenue; the building is recorded directly in net assets
As a capital contribution in a separate statement
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions of $1,500,000
exp: ASU 2016-14 eliminated the option to imply a time restriction on donated long-lived assets; absent donor stipulations, the contribution is reported without donor restrictions. Releasing it over the useful life was the old implied-time-restriction policy.

q: In Year 1, Wellness Center received $80,000 restricted by the donor for the purchase of medical equipment. In Year 2, it bought the equipment and placed it in service; the donor made no other stipulations. When are the net assets released from restriction?
choices: Over the equipment's useful life as it is depreciated
When the equipment is acquired and placed in service in Year 2
When the cash is received in Year 1
Never; the equipment remains in net assets with donor restrictions
exp: Under the placed-in-service approach required by ASU 2016-14, a restriction to acquire long-lived assets expires when the asset is placed in service, absent explicit donor stipulations. Releasing over the useful life required an implied time restriction policy that is no longer allowed.

q: Under ASU 2016-14, what information about liquidity must a not-for-profit organization disclose?
choices: Only the amount of cash at year-end
A statement of cash flows using the direct method
Qualitative information on how it manages liquid resources and quantitative information on the availability of financial assets to meet general expenditures within one year
A projected budget for the next three years
exp: ASU 2016-14 requires qualitative and quantitative liquidity disclosures about financial assets available for general expenditures within one year of the balance sheet date. The direct method is encouraged but not required.

q: On December 31, Year 1, Shelter Inc. received unconditional pledges of $500,000 collectible in 3 years. It estimates 10% will be uncollectible. The present value factor at an appropriate 5% rate for 3 years is 0.8638. What contribution revenue should Shelter recognize in Year 1?
exp: Pledges are measured at the present value of the estimated cash flows to be collected: $500,000 x 90% x 0.8638 = $388,710 (ASC 958-310). $431,900 discounts the pledges but ignores the expected uncollectible amounts.

q: How should a not-for-profit organization measure its investments in equity securities with readily determinable fair values?
choices: At cost, with impairment losses recognized
At the lower of cost or market
Using the equity method, regardless of ownership percentage
At fair value, with gains and losses reported in the statement of activities
exp: ASC 958-320 requires such equity securities and all debt securities to be measured at fair value, with gains and losses reported in the statement of activities as changes in net assets. Unlike business entities, NFPs have no available-for-sale OCI category.

q: A pharmaceutical company donated medical supplies with a fair value of $25,000 to Health Clinic, an NFP, which used all of them in its patient care program during the year. How should the clinic report the donation?
choices: Disclosure only
Contribution revenue of $25,000 only
Contribution revenue of $25,000 and program expense of $25,000
A reduction of program expenses of $25,000
exp: Contributed nonfinancial assets are recognized as contribution revenue at fair value, and expense is recognized when the supplies are used in the program; ASU 2020-07 also requires them to be presented as a separate line item. Disclosure alone omits a recognizable contribution.

q: Under the functional classification of expenses for a not-for-profit organization, how should the salaries of the accounting and payroll staff be classified?
choices: Program services
Management and general (a supporting service)
Fundraising (a supporting service)
Membership development
exp: Supporting services include management and general, fundraising, and membership development; general administration such as accounting and payroll is management and general. These activities do not directly carry out the organization's mission programs.

q: Trinity Church is the irrevocable beneficiary of a perpetual trust held and controlled by a bank. Trinity will receive the trust's income forever but can never receive the principal. How should Trinity account for its beneficial interest when the trust is established?
choices: No recognition, because a third party controls the trust
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions equal to expected first-year income
Disclosure only
An asset and contribution revenue with donor restrictions (perpetual in nature), measured at the fair value of the beneficial interest
exp: Under ASC 958-605, a beneficiary of a perpetual trust held by a third party recognizes its beneficial interest at fair value as contribution revenue with donor restrictions of a perpetual nature. Distributions received later are reported as investment income.

q: For the year, Elm Society had contributions without donor restrictions of $800,000, contributions with donor restrictions of $300,000, net assets released from restrictions of $200,000, and total expenses of $900,000. What is the change in net assets without donor restrictions?
exp: Without donor restrictions: $800,000 + $200,000 released - $900,000 expenses = $100,000. $200,000 is the change in total net assets ($1,100,000 - $900,000), which wrongly includes the restricted contributions.

q: Under ASU 2018-08, what distinguishes a donor-imposed condition from a donor-imposed restriction?
choices: A condition limits how the assets may be used; a restriction creates a barrier to receiving them
Conditions apply only to cash gifts; restrictions apply only to noncash gifts
A condition includes a barrier to be overcome and a right of return or release from obligation; a restriction limits the use of the assets but does not prevent recognition
There is no difference; both delay revenue recognition
exp: A conditional contribution has both a measurable barrier and a right of return of assets or release from the promisor's obligation; revenue is deferred until the condition is met. A restriction only limits use, so revenue is recognized immediately in net assets with donor restrictions.

q: State law and the donor's terms require that a university's endowment investment gains remain in the endowment until appropriated for expenditure by the board. How should the university classify the current year's investment gains on the donor-restricted endowment?
choices: Without donor restrictions, because the gains are not part of the original gift
With donor restrictions until appropriated for expenditure
As a liability until appropriated
In other comprehensive income
exp: Under ASC 958-205 (UPMIFA guidance), earnings on donor-restricted endowments are classified with donor restrictions until appropriated for expenditure and any purpose restrictions are met. NFPs do not report other comprehensive income.

q: During the year, a local business let Aid Network, an NFP, use office space rent-free; the fair rental value was $24,000. How should Aid Network report the donated use of the space?
choices: Disclosure only
Rent expense of $24,000 only
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions of $24,000, never released
Contribution revenue of $24,000 and rent expense of $24,000
exp: The contributed use of facilities is a contribution of a nonfinancial asset measured at fair rental value, and the space is used as received, so revenue and an equal rent (occupancy) expense are recognized. Expense without revenue would leave the contribution unrecorded.

q: A longtime supporter informed Arts Council that she has named the council as a beneficiary of $1,000,000 in her will. The supporter is alive and the will can be changed at any time. How should Arts Council account for this information?
choices: No recognition, because an intention to give that can be revoked is not an unconditional promise
Contribution revenue of $1,000,000 at present value
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions of $1,000,000
A receivable disclosed in the notes at $1,000,000
exp: A revocable bequest is an intention to give, not an unconditional promise, so it is not recognized until the donor dies and the estate is probated (ASC 958-605-25-8). Recognizing it at present value treats it as a pledge.
